title: Teaching Syllabus
excerpt: To study Buddhism is to practice, and to practice exactly as the Buddha taught.

inline.s: To study Buddhism is to practice, and to practice exactly as the Buddha taught.
In its cultivation there is a step by which to enter;
in its realization there is a truth one obtains for oneself.
Diligent and enduring, with a correct method, pressing on without faltering.

The training objectives of the Chan School: to understand the supreme meaning, to bring ten thousand thoughts into one, to return the one to nothingness, to transcend words and thought, and to hold concentration and wisdom in equal practice; to grasp firmly the basic theories of the Dharma and to be able to read the original texts of the scriptures and treatises directly, thereby laying a solid foundation for spreading the Dharma and benefiting living beings.
[Supreme Meaning] The supreme, unsurpassed principle, namely the true mark of all dharmas. The Buddha says:
"All dharmas are false; where they cease, that is called the real, called the true mark, called the Dharma-realm, called ultimate wisdom, called the supreme truth, called the supreme emptiness."
(The Mahaparinirvana Sutra)
The Buddha-Treasury Sutra says:
"The anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Buddhas is wholly without thought and without conception."
It also says:
"Uprooting the root of all conceptual elaboration, forever apart from all, cool and without smoke."
The Essentials of Mind Transmission says:
"When thoughts rest and deliberation is forgotten, the Buddha appears of himself."
Our school's ethos: believe in cause and effect, be able to endure hardship, and never deceive yourself.
[Believing in Cause and Effect]
Master Yinguang says:

"Cause and effect is the great expedient by which the sages govern the world and the Buddhas deliver living beings. Spoken in terms of the Dharma, from the ground of ordinary beings up to the fruit of Buddhahood, no dharma falls outside cause and effect."

(From the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, Preface to the Record of Curing Both the Root and the Branch to Save the World and Men's Hearts.) Plant melons and you get melons, plant beans and you get beans; as the cause, so the fruit. People commit evil because they do not believe in cause and effect. If a student of Buddhism does not deeply believe in cause and effect and carry it out in daily practice, everything becomes idle talk. Elder Master Xuyun says:

"No matter who you are, and especially if you want to apply effort to practicing the Way, you must first deeply believe in cause and effect. If you do not believe in cause and effect and act recklessly, then never mind that your practice of the Way will not succeed: the three evil paths will not be short of you."

(From the Chan Hall Instruction.) [The three evil paths] Also called the three destinies: the destiny of blood, the destiny of knives, and the destiny of fire. The destiny of blood is the animal realm, for animals are constantly in places where they are killed or devour one another; the destiny of knives is the realm of hungry ghosts, for hungry ghosts are constantly in places of hunger or of the pressing of swords, blades, and staves; the destiny of fire is the hell realm, for hells are constantly in places of freezing ice or of the scorching of fierce fire. These three destinies are another name for the three evil paths.
[Enduring Hardship]
To be able to hold out through dry, dull, and arduous training of great intensity.
"The sword's keen edge is ground and ground; the plum's sweet fragrance from bitter cold is found."
Life needs tempering: ceaselessly challenging oneself and surpassing oneself.
[Never Deceiving Yourself]
Do not deceive yourself. Master Hanshan says:
"Since you have roused faith, you should practice in real earnest
(that is, you should actually practice as the Buddha taught)
, and never deceive yourself."
(From the Collection of Dream-Wandering, Instruction to the Daoists of Yihua.) It is said:
"To catch sparrows with the eyes covered is to deceive oneself."

Even a small creature cannot be taken by deceit and self-satisfaction, let alone the great matter of birth-and-death! [Catching sparrows with the eyes covered] Catching sparrows with the eyes blindfolded. A metaphor for deceiving oneself. [Even a small creature cannot be taken by deceit and self-satisfaction, let alone the great matter of birth-and-death] If even the small matter of catching sparrows can never be accomplished through self-deceit, how much less could the great matter of ending birth-and-death be accomplished through self-deceit?

The purpose of studying Buddhism is to seek the Buddha-way above and to transform living beings below. This too is the great mission of every student of Buddhism. How, then, is this purpose to be attained and this mission fulfilled?

In studying Buddhism one must first rouse the bodhi mind, for rousing the bodhi mind is the solemn vow of the great mission of attaining Buddhahood and delivering living beings; it is the lighthouse for crossing the sea of birth-and-death, and the driving force that rides the wind and breaks the waves.
Master Chewu says:
"If the great mind
(the bodhi mind)

is not roused, then outwardly one cannot resonate with the Buddhas, and inwardly one cannot accord with the inherent nature; above, one cannot perfect the Buddha-way, and below, one cannot widely benefit living beings. How shall the love and affection of beginningless time be freed? How shall the grievances and offenses of beginningless time be dissolved? The karmic offenses of accumulated kalpas are hard to purge by repentance. The roots of goodness of accumulated kalpas are hard to bring to maturity. Whatever one practices, one meets many obstructive conditions. Even if something is accomplished, one finally falls into the partial and small. Therefore one must rouse the great bodhi mind in accord with the inherent nature."
(The Posthumous Collection of Master Chewu)
Master Xing'an's Exhortation to Rouse the Bodhi Mind says:

"The essential gate of entering the Way puts rousing the mind first; the urgent task of practice puts establishing the vow before all. Once the vow is established, living beings can be delivered; once the mind is roused, the Buddha-way can be accomplished. If one does not rouse the vast mind and establish a firm vow, then though one pass through dust-like kalpas, one still remains within the round of rebirth; though one may practice, it is all vain toil and hardship. Therefore the Avatamsaka Sutra says: 'To forget and lose the bodhi mind while cultivating all wholesome dharmas is called the work of Mara.' If forgetting it is already so, how much more never having roused it? Thus we know that one who wishes to study the Tathagata's vehicle must first rouse the bodhisattva vow in full, and must not delay."
Peng Jiqing's Preface to the Posthumous Writings of Master Xing'an says:

"Long ago, when our World-Honored One first accomplished perfect enlightenment, he exclaimed: 'How wondrous! How wondrous! There is no living being who is not endowed with the Tathagata's wisdom. It is only because of deluded thinking, inversion, and attachment that they cannot realize it. If they were free of deluded thinking, then all-wisdom, natural wisdom, and unobstructed wisdom would appear before them.' I could never understand
(I could never understand)
why these living beings cling so bitterly to deluded thinking and attachment and do not let them go, or why, with regard to the Tathagata's wisdom, they shrink
(dan, to flinch at difficulty)
from realizing it. In the end
(zu, finally)

they abandon their father and flee away, drifting for long kalpas, content to be a hired servant and a lowly person, and never think of turning back? There is no other reason: they are simply unawakened. The bodhi mind is another name for awakening. No sooner are they awake than the deluded thinking and attachment before them are wholly the Tathagata's wisdom. For the Tathagata's wisdom has no substance of its own, but takes the deluded thinking of living beings as its substance; and the deluded thinking of living beings has no substance of its own, but takes the Tathagata's wisdom as its substance. It is as when water becomes waves: all the waves are water. From the very beginning they are ultimately to dwell in nirvana without residue. Yet the distinction between awakening and non-awakening must never be concealed from or muddled by oneself. When one is startled into reflection on this
(xu, the sound of flesh parting from bone)

and in a crack of sudden understanding, then the rousing of the bodhi mind comes of itself, swelling forth irresistibly. Once this mind is roused, all-wisdom, natural wisdom, and unobstructed wisdom appear before one; what need is there to seek anything else?"
Elder Master Xuyun says:
"To practice is but this: to know the road's head, whence the way must go; once the road's head is truly known, both birth and death at once are done."
The Surangama Sutra says:
"If the causal ground is not true, the fruit comes crooked and askew."

Therefore it is of the utmost importance that a student of Buddhism possess right knowledge and right view. The curriculum of our school is arranged precisely so that, through systematic study and practice, one establishes right knowledge and right view and carries it out in actual conduct.

Its study is divided into four stages: 1. Ceasing evil and practicing good; 2. Taking precepts as the foundation; 3. Prajna destroying delusion; 4. Concentration and wisdom in equal practice. The specific courses are shown in the table below:

inline.s: Studying Buddhism is a process of turning evil into good, delusion into awakening, and the ordinary into the sage; therefore the study of scriptures and treatises must in the end be carried out in actual practice (in thought and in action).

The method of study and practice is: hearing, then reflection, then cultivation. Hearing means hearing the teachings (including reading the teachings); reflection means reflecting on the meaning of the teachings; cultivation means actually practicing in accord with the meaning of the teachings. Through this process our ignorant views are transformed into right knowledge and right view and carried out in body (action), speech, and mind. In this process permeation is very important: only through constant permeation can one awaken to the Buddha's knowledge and view, give rise to wisdom-understanding, and guide one's own actions.

For beginners, starting directly from the original texts of the scriptures and treatises is quite difficult; it is best to begin with annotated editions. Once one has a certain capacity, one should read the original texts directly, for in this way wisdom-understanding more easily arises. Therefore, when studying with annotated editions, one should consciously cultivate the ability to read the original texts directly. The teaching materials of our school are designed exactly for this: to help the reader understand the scriptures and treatises annotated, and at the same time to cultivate the ability to read the original texts of other scriptures and treatises directly. inline.s: The way of study and practice in our school is: self-study, self-discipline, and self-verification, fulfilling well the four great links of faith, understanding, practice, and realization.

The study and practice of our school is divided into two great parts: the study of scriptures and treatises, and meditation. The teaching materials for the study of scriptures and treatises are the books listed in the curriculum table. Meditation is divided into two gates, contemplating the mind and investigating Chan; the teaching material for contemplating the mind is The Essential Mind of White Cloud (The Precious Book of Mind Contemplation), and the teaching material for investigating Chan is the book Awareness Chan.

The process of study and practice is: hearing, then reflection, then cultivation. Hearing means hearing the teachings; reflection means reflecting on the meaning of the teachings; cultivation means actually practicing in accord with the meaning of the teachings. This process is meant to transform our ignorant views into right knowledge and right view and to carry them out in body (action), speech, and mind. In this process permeation is very important: only through constant permeation can one awaken to the Buddha's knowledge and view, give rise to wisdom-understanding, and guide one's own actions.
In
the three studies of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, precepts are the foundation; one must strictly observe the five precepts and the ten wholesome acts.

[The Three Studies] The study of precepts, the study of concentration, and the study of wisdom. Precepts are the prohibitions, which can prevent people from committing all evil karma of body, speech, and mind; concentration is meditative stillness, which can quiet people's reflections and clarify their minds; wisdom is insight, which can enable people to discover the truth and cut off delusion. By cultivating these three studies one can attain concentration through precepts and give rise to wisdom through concentration, and finally gain the undefiled fruit of the Way; therefore the three studies are also called the "three undefiled studies." [Undefiled] Defilement is another name for affliction, with the meaning of leakage. Afflictions such as greed and anger leak and stream out day and night through the six sense-gates such as eye and ear without cease: this is called defilement. Again, defilement has the meaning of falling away; afflictions can make one fall away into the three evil paths: this is called defilement. Hence dharmas accompanied by affliction are called "with defilement," and dharmas apart from affliction are called "undefiled." [The Five Precepts] Not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not lying, and not drinking alcohol. Not killing means not taking the life of living creatures; not stealing means not taking others' property; not committing sexual misconduct means not performing sexual acts outside marriage; not lying means not speaking deceitful and cheating words; not drinking alcohol means not consuming alcoholic drinks or drugs that numb the human mind. [The Ten Wholesome Acts] Ten kinds of wholesome karma, namely: not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not lying, not speaking with a divisive tongue, not speaking harshly, not speaking idly, not being greedy, not being angry, and not being deluded. [Divisive tongue] Carrying tales and setting others at odds. [Idle speech] Filthy and defiling speech, meaningless speech, and words with lewd intent.

inline.s: The study and practice of our school is divided into two great parts: the study of scriptures and treatises, and the Chan of awareness. The teaching materials for the study of scriptures and treatises are the books listed in the curriculum table.
When studying a teaching material, first divide it into a number of units, for example by chapter or section.
First, for each unit:
. Skimming. Read the material of this unit three times to build an overall understanding and to know clearly what the specific content of this unit is.
. Close reading. Divide it into paragraphs, write out the gist of each paragraph and the central idea of this unit, and be clear and lucid about difficult characters and difficult sentences.

. Intensive reading. Through intensive reading, the meaning of technical terms must be remembered, one must be able to recite the essential sentences and verses, and one must be able to expound this unit, especially its difficult points and difficult sentences.
Then:
. Mastering the whole book. The requirements are: write out the central idea and the thread of the whole book, and be able to summarize the whole book without looking at the text.

. Permeation. Through constant permeation, awaken to the Buddha's knowledge and view, give rise to wisdom-understanding, and guide one's own actions. This step is very important: one must constantly examine, transform, and elevate oneself amid circumstances and conditions.

The methods of meditation fall into two great gates, contemplating the mind and investigating Chan. Their common path of practice is: ten thousand thoughts converge into one (subduing affliction), the one returns to nothingness, illuminating the mind and seeing one's nature (severing the delusion of view), severing affliction (severing the delusion of thought), attaining the patient acceptance of non-arising, and perfectly realizing the fruit of Buddhahood.

[Illuminating the Mind and Seeing One's Nature] Illuminating the mind means extinguishing mental thoughts; illuminating the mind and seeing one's nature means extinguishing mental thoughts and thoroughly perceiving the inherent nature. [Extinguishing Mental Thoughts] Mental thoughts are of three kinds: coarse thought, fine thought, and subtlest thought. For example, for one who recites the Buddha's name, deluded thoughts are coarse thought, and the thought of reciting the Buddha's name is fine thought. Ordinarily, when both coarse and fine thought have subsided, this is called no-thought, and this is what is generally meant by no-thought. Further, if the subtlest thought also comes to rest, this is ultimate no-thought. Therefore the meaning of the term "no-thought" must be determined according to context. [Subtlest Thought] The subtle arising, ceasing, and flowing of the consciousness-mind is the mark of the alaya-consciousness. When the subtlest thought temporarily rests, the self-nature presents its inherent-nature state: this is illuminating the mind and seeing one's nature. When the subtlest thought rests forever, one perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.

[Delusion of View] The delusion of view is the confusion and error of ordinary beings with regard to views, such as the five wrong views: the view of self, extreme views, wrong views, the view of grasping at views, and the view of grasping at precepts and prohibitions. [Delusion of Thought] The delusion of thought is the confusion and error of ordinary beings with regard to thinking, such as the afflictions of greed, anger, delusion, pride, and doubt; severing it, one can end birth-and-death and escape the three realms. [Patient Acceptance of Non-Arising] Also called the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas: one understands that all dharmas are from the outset not born, that sentient and insentient alike are condition-born and without nature, and in their very substance are empty; therefore within dharmas without nature the mind rests unmoved in acceptance, personally realizing non-arising.

For details of contemplating the mind, see the teaching material The Essential Mind of White Cloud (The Precious Book of Mind Contemplation); for details of investigating Chan, see the teaching material Awareness Chan.

2. Close reading. Divide it into paragraphs, write out the gist of each paragraph and the central idea of this chapter, and be clear and lucid about difficult characters and difficult sentences.
3. Intensive reading. Through intensive reading, be able to recite the essential sentences, and be able to expound this chapter, especially its difficult sentences and key points.

4. Actual practice. Focused, continuous, and lasting awareness is the common foundation of contemplating the mind and investigating Chan. The schedule is therefore as follows: in the first academic year, be aware of movements and be aware of sensations; in the second academic year, be aware of the breath; in the third and fourth academic years, be aware of the mind's thoughts; in the fifth and sixth academic years, contemplate the mind or investigate Chan. Awareness of movements, awareness of sensations, awareness of the breath, and awareness of the mind's thoughts are described in detail in the preliminary section of Awareness Chan. For details of contemplating the mind, see the teaching material The Essential Mind of White Cloud (The Precious Book of Mind Contemplation); for details of investigating Chan, see the teaching material Awareness Chan. As for the specific methods of study and practice and the points requiring attention, these are explained in detail in The Essential Mind of White Cloud (The Precious Book of Mind Contemplation) and Awareness Chan, and their guiding principle is: start from the difficult, start from the strict, start from actual combat.

blocks.text: 4. The Secret of Success in Study and Practice

inline.s: The secret of success in study and practice: a strong aspiration (as if putting out a fire on one's head), a correct method, and diligent study, hard training, focus, and realization. Start from the difficult and the strict, start from actual combat, and train with a great volume of practice. Practice and apply again and again, press on in the face of difficulty, and amid challenges constantly strengthen your confidence and courage and temper your mental resilience. When tired, when sleepy, when in difficulty, encourage yourself; when temptation comes, when anger rises, when things are dry, dull, and tasteless, admonish yourself: without resolve and willpower, a person accomplishes nothing!

The appearance of difficulty is precisely the turning point of progress. Face difficulty squarely, find the way to solve it, and strive to carry it out, and there will be a new breakthrough. So long as the method is appropriate, together with diligent study and hard training, anyone can achieve outstanding success in study and practice. This is the golden broad road that the patriarchs and great masters have pointed out to us over a thousand years by their own example.

In general, since the way of study and practice is self-study and self-cultivation, you are your own coach, and therefore self-discipline and self-verification are especially important. You must be strict with yourself, control your progress and the results of your practice well, and by all means avoid alternating one day of effort with ten days of neglect, and avoid cooking rice that is half raw. It is very helpful to recall often how you studied when you were at school: how the courses were arranged, how the teachers explained, and how you reviewed, how you completed your assignments, and how you passed the examinations.

The living beings of the Saha world have the sharpest faculty of the ear. Listening while reading is often easier to understand and remember than reading alone. Therefore, when no video of the teaching materials is yet available, one may use a voice-reading tool to read the teaching materials aloud and listen while reading. What is more, one can also permeate one's practice by listening repeatedly.

A voice-reading tool is a tool that helps us learn. Like other tools, the more often it is used, the more proficient one becomes, the more marked the results, and the better one can apply it to the point. If you are not very familiar with installing and adjusting software, ask a friend who is familiar with it to help, and you need only use it. The first stage of the curriculum is "ceasing evil and cultivating virtue," the second stage is "taking precepts and concentration as the foundation," the third stage is "prajna destroying delusion," and the fourth stage is "concentration and wisdom in equal practice."

inline.s: The courses of study at this stage are: the Sutra of the Original Vows of Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva, Liao Fan's Four Lessons, the Record of Mr. Yu Jingyi's Encounter with the Kitchen God, and the Treatise on Response and Retribution. The core of the study is: "Support and serve your parents, serve and attend upon your teachers, cherish compassion and do not kill, and cultivate the ten wholesome acts."

The teaching materials are: Lecture Record on the Sutra of the Original Vows of Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva, Annotated Liao Fan's Four Lessons, Annotated Record of Mr. Yu Jingyi's Encounter with the Kitchen God, and Annotated Treatise on Response and Retribution.

Actual practice: 1. Hearing, reflection, and cultivation; 2. Recite one copy of the Sutra of the Original Vows of Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva every day; 3. Recite the holy name of Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva ten thousand times; 4. Be aware of movements (for details, see the book Awareness Chan).
Introduction to the teaching materials:

rows.s: Lecture Record on the Sutra of the Original Vows of Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva

With the peerless power of his vow, "Only when all living beings are delivered will I realize bodhi; only when the hells are empty will I attain Buddhahood," Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva delivers us suffering living beings. Reciting the Sutra of the Original Vows of Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva not only averts calamity and hardship, dissolves enmity and unties knots, and makes all one does auspicious, but also brings many, many inconceivable merits and benefits.
This book explains the Sutra of the Original Vows of Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva in detail and is a very good guide for study and practice.
Annotated Liao Fan's Four Lessons

Liao Fan's Four Lessons is a precious book for remaking one's destiny; for four hundred years countless people of lofty purpose have taken it as their standard, and thereby completely changed their own destinies.

This book provides detailed annotation, helping on the one hand to understand the meaning of the original text, and on the other hand helping students to improve their ability to read classical Chinese, thus laying a foundation for reading the scriptures and treatises directly.
Annotated Record of Mr. Yu Jingyi's Encounter with the Kitchen God

The Record of Mr. Yu Jingyi's Encounter with the Kitchen God is a companion piece to Liao Fan's Four Lessons, and is likewise a precious book for remaking one's destiny; for four hundred years countless people of lofty purpose have taken it as their standard, and thereby completely changed their own destinies.

This book provides detailed annotation, helping on the one hand to understand the meaning of the original text, and on the other hand helping students to improve their ability to read classical Chinese, thus laying a foundation for reading the scriptures and treatises directly.
Records of Wang Fengyi's Excellent Words

The Records of Wang Fengyi's Excellent Words are the recorded sayings of the venerable good man Wang Fengyi (1864-1937). He was a hired farmhand in the countryside who had never attended school, yet because he earnestly practiced loyalty and filial piety, he became enlightened through sincerity. At the age of thirty-five, on his way to rescue his friend Yang Bo, a strange sign appeared in the heavens midway, and in the black night he saw bright day, whereupon he understood the Way. At thirty-eight his father passed away, and after keeping vigil at the grave for a hundred days he attained great awakening; he then devised the method of healing illness through the principle of the nature, explaining illness to transform the world and universally delivering the multitude. When the good man Wang spoke of the Way, his words seemed homely and plain, yet their meaning was profound, all flowing forth from the inherent nature; unbound by scriptures and teachings, he taught with expedient means, lively and natural, and his essential aim was to teach people to fulfill the way of loyalty and filial piety, transform their nature, and establish their destiny. Wang Fengyi tells us: wealth and honor or poverty and lowliness, good fortune or misfortune, suffering or joy in life are all held in one's own hands.
Annotated Treatise on Response and Retribution

Master Yinguang says: "The Treatise of the Most High on Response and Retribution gathers the supreme principles that blessing follows the good and calamity the perverse, that virtue brings reward and license brings ruin, and gives them forth in arguments that shake heaven and earth and startle the eye and heart. What is good? What is evil? What good reward does the doer of good receive? What evil reward does the doer of evil receive? It penetrates the root and source, clear as looking at a person. Moreover, the reason foolish people refuse to do good and do evil at will is that a selfish, self-seeking heart drives them to it. Now they know that the selfish and self-seeking instead lose great benefit and gain great calamity; would they dare not strive to do good, hoping that calamity may be extinguished and blessing gathered? From this we may say that this book benefits people deeply! Hence many great Confucian scholars of old cultivated themselves in secret according to it. ... To speak of this book in the ultimate, it stops at becoming an immortal; but if one practices it with the great bodhi mind, one can transcend the ordinary and enter the sage, end birth-and-death, sever the three delusions and realize the dharmakaya, perfect blessing and wisdom and accomplish the Buddha-way; how much more so than the mere human and heavenly small fruit of becoming an immortal!" (Preface to the Direct Explanation of the Treatise of the Most High on Response and Retribution)
